# Operate a decentralised Zone with round-robin sequencer rotation

#### Get started with multi-sequencer channels using the Zone SDK and round-robin slot windows.

> **Tip: Version**
>
> This document is accurate for **Testnet v0.3**.

This tutorial covers how to configure and operate a [Logos Blockchain](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#logos-blockchain) [channel](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#channel) with a committee of accredited sequencers that take turns publishing inscriptions to a Logos [Zone](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#zone). It is intended for zone developers using the [Zone SDK](https://github.com/logos-blockchain/logos-blockchain/tree/0.3.2/zone-sdk) who need to move from a single-sequencer setup to a decentralised one.

The Zone SDK currently supports **round-robin** rotation only. Each sequencer publishes inscriptions for `posting_timeframe` slots before the rotation advances to the next sequencer in the `accredited_keys` list. Other scheduling schemes (such as First-Write-Wins) are not yet available.

> **Info: Prerequisites**
>
>
> - An existing application using the Zone SDK, such as an [inscription program](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/zone-sdk/inscribe-data-on-chain-using-zone-sdk.md).
> - At least one `Ed25519PublicKey` generated per committee member.

## What to expect

- You can publish inscriptions from any sequencer at any time; the SDK holds pending transactions and drains them automatically when the sequencer's turn arrives.
- You can monitor each sequencer's turn status in real time using `subscribe_turn_to_write` or `subscribe_channel_view`.
- You can update the accredited key list to add or remove sequencers by submitting a `ChannelConfigOp`.

## Step 1: Size the rotation parameters

Choose values for `posting_timeframe` and `posting_timeout` before creating or reconfiguring the channel. These fields on [`ChannelState`](https://lip.logos.co/blockchain/raw/bedrock-v1.1-mantle-specification.html#message-ordering) control the rotation cadence and inactive-sequencer skip behaviour.

> **Info**
>
> The [Mantle specification](https://lip.logos.co/blockchain/raw/bedrock-v1.1-mantle-specification.html) is the source of truth for the exact rotation algorithm. The guidance below is a practical summary.

1. Set `posting_timeframe` - the length of each sequencer's turn under normal circumstances - to at least the average slots-per-block of the Logos Blockchain.

   - A turn shorter than one block lets multiple sequencers become authorised within the same block, defeating the purpose of rotation.
   - As a rule of thumb, use a multiple: with a ~20 slots/block average, `posting_timeframe = 60` gives each sequencer roughly three blocks of ownership per turn.

1. Set `posting_timeout` to a value greater than or equal to `posting_timeframe`. `posting_timeout` is the time we wait for an inactive sequencer to publish before continuing to the next sequencer - all subsequent inactive sequencers have a turn of `posting_timeout` slots until one of them publishes. At that point, turns go back to being `posting_timeframe` slots long.

   - Values smaller than `posting_timeframe` make the timeout branch dominate cadence as soon as the authorised sequencer goes silent.

1. Confirm the worked example matches your intended behaviour before proceeding.

   A channel with three accredited keys, `posting_timeframe = 60`, and `posting_timeout = 180`:

   ```
   slots 0–59     → index 0
   slots 60–119   → index 1
   slots 120–179  → index 2
   slots 180–239  → index 0
   ...
   ```

   > **Info**
   >
   > The Zone SDK exposes the current rotation state to your sequencer in two forms:
   >
   > - The full `SequencerChannelView` (`subscribe_channel_view`)—a `tokio::sync::watch` receiver carrying `authorized_key_index`, `own_key_index`, `our_turn_to_write`, the current [slot](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#slot), and the turn window's `turn_to_write_slots`.
   > - A focused `TurnNotification` (`subscribe_turn_to_write`) plus `Event::TurnNotification`—emitted only when the turn boundary actually changes.
   >
   > `our_turn_to_write` is the boolean a sequencer reads to decide whether it is currently authorised.

## Step 2: Publish inscriptions and monitor turn state

The Zone SDK queues inscriptions locally when it is not your sequencer's turn and posts them automatically when the turn arrives. You do not need to gate `publish` calls on turn state yourself.

1. Call `publish` from any task at any time.

   ```rust
   // From the drive task, once `Event::Ready` has fired.
   let (result, checkpoint) = sequencer.handle().publish(zone_block).await?;
   // `result.tx` is a `PendingTx::Inscription(...)`.
   // `checkpoint` is up to date with the new pending entry.
   // The post may not have hit the node yet if it is not our turn.
   ```

   - The SDK enqueues the transaction immediately if it is your turn and posts to the network.
   - The SDK enqueues the transaction with `posted: false` if it is not your turn; it drains automatically when the turn arrives.
   - A periodic `resubmit_interval` (default 30 s) re-drains pending publishes if your turn is current, covering transient network failures.

1. Subscribe to turn notifications to drive your UI or application logic. Choose one of the two surfaces based on your use case:

   - Use `TurnNotification` (edge-triggered) to wake the UI only when the turn boundary changes:

     ```rust
     use lb_zone_sdk::sequencer::Event;

     if let Event::TurnNotification { notification } = event {
         if notification.our_turn_to_write {
             println!(
                 "Our turn until slot {:?}",
                 notification.ends_at_slot,
             );
         } else {
             println!(
                 "Waiting for our turn; current authorized window ends at {:?}",
                 notification.ends_at_slot,
             );
         }
     }
     ```

   - Use `subscribe_channel_view` (snapshot) to read the full rotation state on every block, for example to render a status panel:

     ```rust
     let view_rx = sequencer.subscribe_channel_view();
     let view = view_rx.borrow().clone();
     if view.our_turn_to_write {
         // Authorized right now.
     } else if let (Some(own), Some(auth)) = (view.own_key_index, view.authorized_key_index) {
         println!(
             "Sequencer {} is publishing; we are sequencer {}.",
             auth, own,
         );
     }
     ```

     The view also carries `pending_publish_txs` and `queued_messages` so the UI can show how many inscriptions are waiting for the next turn.

1. Handle competing writes by listening for `Event::BlocksProcessed` events and checking `channel_update.orphaned()` for orphaned transactions. Republish these transactions with the latest parent.

   > **Info**
   >
   > Two sequencers can race on the same parent slot during rotation transitions or after a resync. The on-chain rule is: the first valid [inscription](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#inscription) wins; the loser's transaction is surfaced in `channel_update.orphaned()`.

   ```rust
   use lb_zone_sdk::sequencer::{ChannelUpdateTx, Event};

   if let Event::BlocksProcessed { channel_update, .. } = event {
       for entry in channel_update.orphaned() {
           if let ChannelUpdateTx::Inscription(info) = entry {
               let (result, checkpoint) = sequencer.handle().publish(info.payload.clone()).await?;
               // Persist `result` + `checkpoint` exactly as on the original publish.
           }
       }
   }
   ```

   - `channel_update` is a `ChannelUpdate` object. It is a `ChannelUpdate::Extension { adopted }` when nothing you hold became invalid, and a `ChannelUpdate::Conflict { common_prefix, adopted, orphaned }` when entries left the channel view. `orphaned()` is empty on an extension.
   - To keep your own state in step with a conflict, either revert every orphaned entry and apply every adopted one, or reset to finalised state and replay `channel_update.canonical_chain()`, the whole non-finalised view at the new tip. Your own publishes are applied at publish time and appear in `adopted` only after they were first reported orphaned.
   - `tests/src/cucumber/steps/zone/operations/policies.rs` in the `logos-blockchain` repository contains reference policies for this republish loop: `OrphanRepublishPolicy` (simple republish), `RepublishLineagePolicy` (for repeating payloads, so each intent lands once), `SortedConflictPolicy` (republish only when it preserves the channel's sorted order), and `BalanceAwarePolicy` (republish only when the account balance still allows it).
   - If the orphan was caused by an application-level conflict rather than a race, you can choose to drop the payload or deduplicate it against a higher-level transaction stream, or apply any other custom rule instead of republishing.

   > **Note**
   >
   > Channel transactions built outside the publish API are classified by shape, not by how they were submitted. One inscription plus at most one funding transfer surfaces as `ChannelUpdateTx::Inscription`; with withdrawals added, as `ChannelUpdateTx::AtomicWithdraw`; with one channel transfer and no withdrawals, as `ChannelUpdateTx::PinDeposit`. A lone channel config surfaces as `ChannelUpdateTx::Config`. Anything else surfaces as `ChannelUpdateTx::Custom(SignedOps)`.
   >
   > For `Custom` entries the SDK hands back the whole transaction, and it is up to the consumer to parse it (the `channel_inscriptions` helper extracts its inscriptions) and decide how to recover it. The main API is `publish`, `publish_atomic_withdraw`, and `publish_pin_deposit`.

   > **Info: Stuck transactions**
   >
   > A pending transaction that stays out of a block for longer than `SequencerConfig::stale_refund_slots` (default 30 slots of the last irreversible block, `0` disables it) is recovered automatically when the SDK can sign it alone. Transactions from `publish`, `publish_atomic_withdraw`, and `publish_pin_deposit` are re-funded, re-signed, and posted again with the same message ID. Multi-signature and custom transactions are shed instead and reported in `orphaned()`, together with everything chained on them, so you prepare them, collect signatures, and submit them again.

## Step 3: Update the committee with a channel config op

Submit a channel config to add or remove sequencers from `accredited_keys`. Because a channel config overwrites the entire key list, you should re-include any keys that should remain accredited after the update.

1. Use `channel_config` directly when `configuration_threshold == 1`, that is, when you only need one sequencer's signature to change the configuration.

   ```rust
   use lb_core::mantle::{
       channel::{SlotTimeframe, SlotTimeout},
       ops::channel::VerifiedChannelKeys,
   };

   let new_keys = VerifiedChannelKeys::from([
       admin_pk,
       new_sequencer_b_pk,
       new_sequencer_c_pk,
   ]);

   let ((result, checkpoint), signed_tx) = sequencer
       .handle()
       .channel_config(
           new_keys,
           SlotTimeframe::from(60), // ~3 blocks per turn at 20 slots/block
           SlotTimeout::from(180),  // skip after 3 turn windows of inactivity
           1,                       // configuration_threshold (still single-admin)
           1,                       // transfer_threshold
       )
       .await?;
   ```

   `channel_config` funds, signs with the local key only, and submits the transaction. On finalisation, the SDK picks up the new config and the next `BlocksProcessed` event recomputes `our_turn_to_write` for every running sequencer.

1. Use the `prepare_channel_config` → `sign_with` → `submit_channel_config` flow when `configuration_threshold > 1`. In this case, collecting signatures from other sequencers is the responsibility of the application rather than the Zone SDK.

   - The proposer calls `prepare_channel_config` with the new configuration. The SDK builds and funds the config transaction and returns a `PreparedChannelConfig`.
   - Each key holder inspects `prepared.tx()` and signs with `prepared.sign_with(&key)`, which returns an `IndexedSignature` indexed against the channel's current accredited keys. A key holder without a running sequencer can call `sign_prepared(&key, &prepared.accredited_keys, &prepared.sign_payload)` instead.
   - The proposer gathers `prepared.signing_threshold` signatures, the channel's current `configuration_threshold`, into `IndexedSignatures` and submits them with `submit_channel_config`.

   ```rust
   use lb_core::mantle::{
       channel::{SlotTimeframe, SlotTimeout},
       ops::channel::VerifiedChannelKeys,
   };
   use lb_zone_sdk::sequencer::{IndexedSignature, IndexedSignatures};

   // 1. Propose the new configuration. The SDK builds and funds the tx.
   let prepared = sequencer
       .handle()
       .prepare_channel_config(
           VerifiedChannelKeys::from([admin_pk, sequencer_b_pk, sequencer_c_pk]),
           SlotTimeframe::from(60),
           SlotTimeout::from(180),
           2, // configuration_threshold
           1, // transfer_threshold
       )
       .await?;

   // 2. Distribute `prepared` to the rest of the committee; each key holder
   //    signs with `prepared.sign_with(&key)`. Transport is application-defined.
   let collected: Vec<IndexedSignature> = collect_signatures_from_committee(&prepared).await?;

   // 3. Gather the signatures, ordered by key index with at most one per key,
   //    and submit.
   let signatures = IndexedSignatures::try_from_iter(collected.into_iter().map(Into::into))?;
   let (result, checkpoint) = sequencer
       .handle()
       .submit_channel_config(prepared, signatures)?;
   ```

   - A signature authorises every channel operation in the prepared transaction, not only the config, so signers should inspect the whole of `prepared.tx()` before signing.
   - A config position holds one pending continuation, so `prepare_channel_config` refuses a second config on a parent that already has one pending until it lands or expires.
   - An orphaned multi-signature config surfaces as `ChannelUpdateTx::Config`. Recover it by running the prepare → collect signatures → submit flow again.

## Next steps

For more examples of what can be built with the Zone SDK, see the following link:

- [Bridge assets between Logos Blockchain and a Zone](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/zone-sdk/bridge-assets-between-blockchain-and-zone.md)

> Source: https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/blend/join-the-blend-network-as-a-core-node
> Markdown index of all Logos docs: https://docs.logos.co/llms.txt

# Join the Blend Network as a core node

#### Connect your blockchain node to Blend to contribute to proposer privacy.

> **Tip: Version**
>
> This document is accurate for **Testnet v0.3.0**.

Joining the [Blend Network](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#blend-network) lets your blockchain node contribute to the privacy of [Logos Blockchain](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#logos-blockchain) proposers and receive rewards for participating. This procedure applies to operators of a running Logos Blockchain node who want to register that node as a Blend [core node](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#core-node). Before you start, make sure your node's address is publicly reachable so other peers can connect to it.

> **Note**
>
> Joining the Blend Network as a core node via a [Basecamp](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/get-started/run-blockchain-node-from-basecamp.md) is not currently supported.
>
> Instead, follow the CLI instructions below, but navigate to your Basecamp Logos Blockchain node's **Generate-Config** screen to find the **Blend port** field. Use this value in place of `<YOUR_BLEND_PORT>`.

> **Info: Prerequisites**
>
>
> - [A running blockchain node](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/get-started/run-blockchain-node-from-cli.md).
> - A publicly reachable IP and port (or DNS) combination for the node.
> - Stable connection (10 Mbps+ recommended) to handle multiple concurrent connections. A stable, low-latency connection is beneficial for effective message blending and random delays.

## What to expect

- Your blockchain node is registered as a Blend core node.
- Your node contributes to [proposer privacy](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#proposer-privacy) and becomes eligible for rewards.
- Your declaration is confirmed on-chain and becomes active after two [epochs](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#epoch).

## Register your node as a Blend core node

Complete these steps to fund the required keys, retrieve a locked [note](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#note), and submit your Blend join declaration.

1.  Start the node and poll until the mode switches to `"Online"`. This takes approximately one hour:

    ```bash
    logosctl call blockchain_module get_cryptarchia_info | jq -r .result.value | jq .mode
    # > "Bootstrapping"

    # ... Wait ~1h, then re-run until you see:
    # > "Online"
    ```

1.  Open your `keystore.yaml` and note the `BlendZk` and `SdpFunding` public keys. Both need funds.

    ```yaml
    # keystore.yaml
    public_keys:
      ...
      BlendZk: 13cccf99f90fd78c2134891ce3c1afce0605753a7694b9d56678d63a8d471820
      ...
      SdpFunding: 91d381a87e05d46fc9bc95246273b6930290506f0589ad039444decd3c24940e
      ...
    ```

1.  Fund both keys by mining. Start mining. Auto-claim pays the mined rewards into your node's `PoWClaim` key, and you then transfer funds from that key to the `BlendZk` and `SdpFunding` keys:

    ```bash
    logosctl call blockchain_module pow_start_mining
    ```

    - The `BlendZk` key needs a single note of at least 1,000,000,000 (1 billion), the minimum stake that the declaration locks.
    - The `SdpFunding` key pays the fees for the declaration and for the activity message your node sends each epoch. Send it at least 50,000,000 (50 million), which covers two months of fees with a wide margin for fee increases.

1.  Check the auto-claim target. Its `public_key` is your `PoWClaim` key, and its `balance` grows as auto-claim collects rewards. Rerun this command periodically until the balance is at least 1,050,000,000 (1.05 billion):

    ```bash
    logosctl call blockchain_module pow_status | jq -r .result.value | jq .auto_claim.targets
    ```

    - With the generated config, auto-claim pays the `PoWClaim` key up to 2,000,000,000 (2 billion), then stops itself and stops mining. You can continue as soon as the balance reaches 1.05 billion, or wait for mining to stop at 2 billion.

    > **Info: How long mining takes**
    >
    > Each claim pays about 2 million, so 1.05 billion takes about 525 claims and 2 billion about 1,000. How fast a node collects claims depends on its CPU and on how many other nodes are mining. On Testnet v0.3.1 in October 2026, a typical node collected about 8 claims an hour, so it reached 1.05 billion in about 3 days and 2 billion in about 5.5 days. The fastest nodes collected about 65 claims an hour and reached 2 billion in about 15 hours. To estimate your own time, check the `balance` an hour apart.

1.  Merge the mined rewards into larger notes. Auto-claim pays each claim as a separate note of about 2 million, but a transfer can spend at most 32 notes, so the 1 billion transfer can't be sent from these small notes directly. This script repeatedly transfers the 32 largest notes of the `PoWClaim` key back to itself as one note, waiting for each transfer to land, until the 32 largest notes together cover the 1 billion transfer plus a margin for its fee. Replace `<POW_CLAIM_KEY>` with the `public_key` from the previous step:

    ```bash
    K=<POW_CLAIM_KEY>; n() { logosctl call blockchain_module wallet_get_notes $K "" | jq -r .result.value | jq "[.notes[].value | tonumber] | sort | reverse | $1"; }
    if [ $(n 'add // 0') -lt 1000100000 ]; then echo "Not enough funds: the key holds $(n 'add // 0'), and merging needs at least 1000100000. Keep mining."; else
    while [ $(n length) -gt 2 ] && [ $(n '.[:32] | add') -lt 1000100000 ]; do a=$(( $(n '.[:32] | add') - 100000 )); logosctl call blockchain_module wallet_transfer_funds $K "json:[\"$K\"]" $K str:$a "" | jq -e .result.success || break; until [ $(n '.[0]') -ge $a ]; do sleep 30; done; done; fi
    ```

    - If the key holds less than 1,000,100,000 in total, the script prints the current balance and stops without sending anything. Keep mining and run it again later.

    - Each round merges up to 32 notes and needs a block to land, so reaching 1 billion takes about 16 rounds. Expect this to take 15 to 30 minutes.
    - Each round pays a fee of about 1,800 at current gas prices.

1.  Transfer 1,000,000,000 (1 billion) from your `PoWClaim` key to the `BlendZk` key, replacing the placeholders with your keys. The `PoWClaim` key pays the fee and receives any change:

    ```bash
    logosctl call blockchain_module wallet_transfer_funds \
      <POW_CLAIM_KEY> 'json:["<POW_CLAIM_KEY>"]' <BLEND_ZK_KEY> str:1000000000 ""

    # A successful call returns the transaction hash:
    # > {"method":"wallet_transfer_funds","module":"blockchain_module","result":{"error":null,"success":true,"value":"<TX_HASH>"},"status":"ok"}
    ```

    - The arguments are, in order: the key that receives any change, the list of keys whose notes pay for the transfer, the recipient key, the amount, and the block to build the transfer on, where `""` means the current tip.
    - The `json:` prefix passes the funding keys as a list, and the `str:` prefix passes the amount as text, which `wallet_transfer_funds` requires. Both prefixes need `logosctl` 0.3.2 or later.

1.  Once the 1 billion transfer has landed, which you can check with `wallet_get_notes` as shown in the next step, transfer the remaining funds to the `SdpFunding` key. Send at least 50,000,000 (50 million):

    ```bash
    logosctl call blockchain_module wallet_transfer_funds \
      <POW_CLAIM_KEY> 'json:["<POW_CLAIM_KEY>"]' <SDP_FUNDING_KEY> str:50000000 ""
    ```

    - One transfer can move about 60 million at most, because it spends at most 32 notes. To move more of the remaining balance, repeat the transfer once the previous one has landed.

1.  Wait until both keys have received funds. Check each balance with `wallet_get_notes`:

    ```bash
    logosctl call blockchain_module wallet_get_notes <ADDRESS> "" \
      | jq -r .result.value | jq .notes
    # > [
    # >   {
    # >     "id": "<BLEND_ZK_NOTE_ID>",
    # >     "value": "1000000000"
    # >   }
    # > ]
    ```

    - Note the `id` of the 1 billion note held by the `BlendZk` key—you need it in the next step.

1.  Join the Blend Network by locking the 1 billion note held by your `BlendZk` key.

    > **Info**
    >
    > Make sure to open `<YOUR_BLEND_PORT>/udp` on the public host firewall before running the following command. `<YOUR_BLEND_PORT>` can be found in `user_config.yaml` under `blend.core.backend.listening_address`. Configure the firewall and NAT forwarding before joining and verify the local listener and public reachability after activation.

    ```sh
    logosctl call blockchain_module blend_join_as_core_node \
       "/ip4/<YOUR_IP>/udp/<YOUR_BLEND_PORT>/quic-v1" \
       "<BLEND_ZK_NOTE_ID>"

    # A successful call will return the declaration id:
    # > {"method":"blend_join_as_core_node","module":"blockchain_module","result":{"error":null,"success":true,"value":"2691821bd61394cc18939626de4e9231c699e8ddefd1ebf9e6c35b32229bdc65"},"status":"ok"}
    ```

    - `<YOUR_IP>`: Must be your external IP address
    - `<YOUR_BLEND_PORT>`: Your configured Blend port from the `user_config.yaml` file (`blend.core.backend.listening_address`). Note that if you do port-mapping, the external mapped port must be used.
    - `<BLEND_ZK_NOTE_ID>`: The ID of the 1 billion note held by your `BlendZk` key, as queried above.
    - The Blend core listener starts only after the node's declaration becomes active.

1.  Confirm the declaration was accepted on-chain by polling `/mantle/sdp/declarations` and looking for your entry:

    ```bash
    curl http://<YOUR_NODE_IP>:8080/mantle/sdp/declarations | jq .
    # > {
    # >   "<DECLARATION_ID>": {
    # >     "service_type": "BN",
    # >     "provider_id": "35d60d973560b8344f83dc266a3fe89e35a3dcf9959c492d0a7a0b7a85c5d2ce",
    # >     "locked_note_id": "<BLEND_ZK_NOTE_ID>",
    # >     "locators": [
    # >       "/ip4/<YOUR_IP>/udp/<YOUR_BLEND_PORT>/quic-v1"
    # >     ],
    # >     "zk_id": "13cccf99f90fd78c2134891ce3c1afce0605753a7694b9d56678d63a8d471820",
    # >     "created": 1,
    # >     "active": 3,
    # >     "withdraw_at": null,
    # >     "nonce": 0
    # >   }
    # > }
    ```

    - The response is a JSON **object keyed by declaration id** (not a list). Find your entry by its `provider_id` (your `BlendSigning` key) or `zk_id` (your `BlendZk` key).
    - `service_type: "BN"` identifies this as a [Blend node](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#blend-node) declaration.
    - `created` is the epoch your declaration was included; it takes effect about two epochs later. `active` is the most recent epoch your node has re-attested activity for (via the periodic Active message), so it **advances over time**—it equals `created + 2` right after activation and grows on a long-running node.
    - If your declaration is not yet listed, retry after your transaction is included in a block.

1. Check the configured Blend UDP listener:

   ```sh
   ss -lun
   ```

   - Confirm that the local UDP port from `blend.core.backend.listening_address` is present. If the public Blend port differs, also confirm that NAT forwards `<YOUR_BLEND_PORT>/udp` to this local port.

## Frequently asked questions

### Did my core declaration land?

After declaring as a core node, query the on-chain SDP declarations and look for your entry:

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:8080/mantle/sdp/declarations
```

Find the entry whose `zk_id` is your BlendZk key, with `"service_type": "BN"`. It will become active a couple of epochs after the declaring transaction is included in a block, and stays active only while the node keeps sending Active messages. 

### Is my node participating in the Blend Network right now?

Check the node log for the Blend [Service](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#service) lifecycle:

```bash
grep -aE "blend::service" <node-log> | tail
```

- `Waiting for chain to become Online mode`—not yet; the node is still [bootstrapping](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#bootstrapping).
- `Chain is now Online`, followed by the Blend Service starting and `Blend edge swarm started with local peer id …`—proposals will be routed through Blend, whether your node is a core node or not.
- `current membership is ready members=N`—the node sees `N` active core nodes this epoch. If `N` is below the minimum needed, the node falls back to [broadcast mode](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/concepts/about-the-blend-network.md#node-roles-core-edge-and-broadcast) for that epoch (no Blend privacy).

There is also an API endpoint, `curl http://localhost:8080/blend/info`, which returns the Blend Network info once the node is Online. Note that it can hang or time out while the node is still bootstrapping (Blend is not up yet), so it is better to use the log check during sync.

> Source: https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/logos-sql
> Markdown index of all Logos docs: https://docs.logos.co/llms.txt

# Introduction to Logos SQL

#### Learn how applications share a database through the Logos Blockchain while keeping a local copy of their data.

> **Tip: Version**
>
> This document is accurate for **Testnet v0.3**.

Logos SQL is a Rust library that gives an application a local SQLite database and synchronises its writes with other participants through the [Logos Blockchain](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#logos-blockchain). Applications can create tables, submit SQL transactions and query their own database, with the Logos SQL library handling replication.

Logos SQL is useful for participants who need shared data without relying on one organisation to host the database for everyone. Each participant maintains its own copy. Different applications can use the same data by following the same channel.

## State and history

There are two ways to describe a database: the data it contains now, and the writes that produced it. Logos SQL connects these two views:

- **Local SQLite holds the current data.** The application can query it without making a network request for each read.
- **Logos Blockchain carries the shared write history.** It determines the accepted writes and their order. Each participant applies that history to its own database.

The blockchain does not execute the SQL. Logos SQL runs it on each participant's machine and uses the [Zone SDK](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/zone-sdk/inscribe-data-on-chain-using-zone-sdk.md) to publish and receive the shared history.

```text
Application A --> Logos SQL A <--> Local SQLite A
                       |
                       |
              Shared channel history
                 Logos Blockchain
                       |
                       |
Application B --> Logos SQL B <--> Local SQLite B
```

Both library instances follow the channel. Instances configured as writers can also publish to it.

## Channels define databases

A [channel](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#channel) is an ordered history of [inscriptions](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#inscription) on the Logos Blockchain. Logos SQL uses these inscriptions to share SQL transactions between participants.

Instances using the same channel follow the same database history, while different channels have separate histories. The channel carries both schema changes, such as creating tables, as well as writes to the data in those tables.

A writer, as a sequencer for the database's channel, needs an authorised signing key and funding for inscription fees, while a read-only instance follows the history without publishing. Channel permission controls who can submit writes; it does not provide separate SQL permissions for individual tables or rows.

## Writes start locally

An application prepares SQL statements and bound parameters, then calls `execute`.

1. Logos SQL runs the transaction against the local database. Its statements commit together or roll back together.
2. After saving the local changes and recovery information, it returns a transaction ID. The application can already read its changes.
3. The library publishes the write in the background. Other participants receive the channel history and apply it locally.
4. When the chain finalises that history, the write becomes part of the finalised database.

A successful `execute` means **committed locally**, not **finalised on the chain**. This keeps the application responsive while publication and agreement happen over the network.

After startup, applications can continue writing locally during a connection outage while there is room in the pending-write queue. If the queue fills, further writes return `PublishPending` without committing their changes. Saved writes remain available for publication when the connection returns, but changes in channel history can displace them. Starting an instance still requires a connection to catch up with channel history.

## Latest vs finalised state

Logos SQL provides two local read connections:

| View | Contents | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Latest | The most up-to-date local state, including writes that are not yet finalised. | Showing and working with recent changes. |
| Finalised | The database produced by finalised channel history. | Decisions that must use settled history. |

The latest state can include changes that are undone when the chain switches branches. Finalised history is not undone by those reorganisations, though later finalised writes can still update its rows.

Participants can temporarily see different data while writes are pending or they are catching up. Applying the same accepted history brings their replicas into agreement.

## Responding to changes in history

Two writers could end up competing for the next inscription in the channel, or a chain reorganisation can remove previously accepted writes. A local write may then lose its place in history even though its SQL was successfully executed.

Logos SQL updates the live database to match the current history. It reports affected local writes as **displaced** and blocks ordinary new writes until the application has considered them. The application can retry the original SQL, continue without retrying it, or prepare a different change.

The library does not automatically decide which action is appropriate. An old update might overwrite a newer value if repeated. A displaced write can also return if its branch becomes canonical again.

See [Handle displaced writes](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/logos-sql/handle-displaced-writes.md) for the application flow and examples of SQL conditions.

## Bootstrapping and restarts

A new participant can build its database from existing channel history via `LogosSql::start`. Another application instance does not have to prepare and send a database export.

Each participant keeps a separate persistent state directory. On restart, it resumes using that directory. Replication runs in the background for as long as the Logos SQL library is running.

## Before building

- **Protect sensitive data before submission.** Logos SQL does not encrypt application SQL or parameter values. Deleting a row does not erase the write from chain history.
- **Submit writes through Logos SQL.** Writes must go through the Logos SQL API to be shared with other participants. Changing the SQLite database directly does not publish those changes.
- **Plan for provisional results.** Use finalised reads where needed, and decide how the application responds to displaced writes.

> **Tip**
>
> Follow [Build an application with Logos SQL](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/logos-sql/build-application-with-logos-sql.md) to run the password-manager example, follow its writes between participants and review displaced writes.

---

> Source: https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/logos-sql/build-application-with-logos-sql
> Markdown index of all Logos docs: https://docs.logos.co/llms.txt

# Build an application with Logos SQL

#### Run a password-manager example and follow its SQL writes between two local databases.

> **Tip: Version**
>
> This document is accurate for **Testnet v0.3**.

This guide demonstrates how Logos SQL can be used to maintain an application's database on the [Logos Blockchain](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#logos-blockchain). It does this by walking through a [password-manager example](https://github.com/logos-blockchain/logos-blockchain/tree/47a65ab3c/logos_sql/examples/password_manager) in the `logos-blockchain` repository. It shows how an application starts Logos SQL, prepares SQL transactions and reads its local database.

The example separates startup configuration, database operations and terminal commands. The same library calls apply to other applications. Read the [introduction](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/logos-sql.md) first for the relationship between local data and shared history.

> **Danger: Use fake credentials only**
>
> The example encrypts accounts, passwords and notes before submitting them to Logos SQL. Labels and write activity remain public. It is a demonstration, not an audited password manager: use fake credentials only. Deleting an entry does not erase its encrypted data from channel history.

The walkthrough uses two instances on your own machine, each with a separate database directory.

> **Info: Prerequisites**
>
>
> - Git, Rust and the [Logos Blockchain build prerequisites](https://github.com/logos-blockchain/logos-blockchain/blob/master/README.md#prerequisites).
> - The OpenSSL command-line tool to generate keys for the example.
> - A compatible Logos Blockchain node that has reached `Online`, with a reachable HTTP API (default: `http://127.0.0.1:8080`). Follow [Run a Logos Blockchain node](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/get-started/run-blockchain-node-from-cli.md) to set one up.
> - A funded key in the node's wallet for [inscription](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#inscription) fees. On a testnet node, follow [Mine tokens to fund your node](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/get-started/run-blockchain-node-from-cli.md#step-4-mine-tokens-to-fund-your-node) to fund the `PoWClaim` key. A local standalone node configures no auto-claim targets, so use the funded genesis key from its `wallet.known_keys` instead, as [Step 2](#step-2-configure-and-start-the-application) sets out.
> - A maximum inscription fee appropriate for your test network.
>

## What to expect

- You can build and run an existing Logos SQL application.
- You can update a fake credential and read it from another participant.
- You can identify the SQL calls and review commands used to handle displaced writes.

## Step 1: Build the example

Logos SQL is not yet published to crates.io. Build the example inside its source workspace.

1. Clone the repository and check out the tested revision:

   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/logos-blockchain/logos-blockchain.git
   cd logos-blockchain
   git checkout 47a65ab3c
   ```

1. Build the password manager:

   ```bash
   cargo build --locked --release -p logos-sql --example password_manager
   ```

1. Check its startup options:

   ```bash
   ./target/release/examples/password_manager --help
   ```

   **Expected result:** help lists the encryption key file, channel, node, signing key, funding key, fee and state-directory options.

## Step 2: Configure and start the application

1. In terminal A, generate a separate encryption key for this example:

   ```bash
   (umask 077; openssl rand -out password-manager.key 32)
   ```

   Run this once, before starting either instance. Do not overwrite an existing key. The file contains 32 random bytes, not a password or a hexadecimal string. Keep it private and backed up: without it, the encrypted data cannot be read. Do not use the channel signing key for encryption.

1. Generate a channel signing key:

   ```bash
   (umask 077; openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out channel-signing.pem)
   ```

   Generate this key only once and keep the file private. Do not overwrite it when restarting or adding a participant. Its public key identifies the new [channel](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#channel); you do not need to create the channel separately.

1. Extract the signing key and channel ID in the hexadecimal format the example accepts:

   ```bash
   export LOGOS_SQL_SIGNING_KEY=$(openssl pkey -in channel-signing.pem -outform DER | tail -c 32 | od -An -tx1 | tr -d ' \n')
   export LOGOS_SQL_CHANNEL_ID=$(openssl pkey -in channel-signing.pem -pubout -outform DER | tail -c 32 | od -An -tx1 | tr -d ' \n')
   ```

   These are 32-byte values without a `0x` prefix. See the [Zone SDK channel setup](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/zone-sdk/inscribe-data-on-chain-using-zone-sdk.md#step-2-initialise-the-zonesequencer-struct) for channel identity and signing authority.

1. Set the remaining values from your test-network setup:

   ```bash
   export LOGOS_SQL_NODE_URL='<node-http-url>'
   export LOGOS_SQL_FUNDING_KEY='<funding-public-key-hex>'
   export LOGOS_SQL_MAX_TX_FEE='<maximum-fee>'
   export LOGOS_SQL_ENCRYPTION_KEY_FILE="$PWD/password-manager.key"
   ```

   Replace every angle-bracket placeholder:
   - For a local node, the default HTTP URL is `http://127.0.0.1:8080`.
   - On a testnet node, use the auto-claim target's `public_key` as the funding key: `pow_status` prints it in [Step 4 of the "Run a Blockchain node" tutorial](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/get-started/run-blockchain-node-from-cli.md#step-4-mine-tokens-to-fund-your-node), and it is also at `pow.auto_claim.targets[0].public_key` in the node's `user_config.yaml`.
   - On a local standalone node, which configures no auto-claim targets, use a funded key from the node's `wallet.known_keys`—check a candidate with `curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/wallet/<key>/balance` first, because the genesis keys are not all funded. The example does not create or fund a wallet.

   > **Note**
   >
   > This walkthrough was tested with example source at commit `47a65ab3c` and `LOGOS_SQL_MAX_TX_FEE=1000000`. This value is a fee cap, not a fixed charge. Required fees can change with network conditions.

1. Start the application with its own state directory:

   ```bash
   ./target/release/examples/password_manager --state-dir ./password-manager-a
   ```

   **Expected result:** after catching up and preparing the schema, it prints:

   ```text
   Password manager is running. Enter `help` to list commands.
   Credentials are encrypted; labels remain public. Use test credentials only.
   password-manager>
   ```

### Understand how it works  

1. Open `logos_sql/examples/password_manager/passwords.rs` and find `PasswordManager::start`:

   ```rust
   /// Starts `λSQL`, catches up with the channel, and prepares the database.
   pub async fn start(config: LogosSqlConfig, encryption: Encryption) -> AppResult<Self> {
      let manager = Self {
         logos_sql: LogosSql::start(config).await?,
         encryption,
      };

      match manager.initialize().await {
         // Keep the terminal available if schema creation was displaced.
         Ok(()) | Err(AppError::LogosSql(LogosSqlError::UnhandledDisplacements)) => {}
         Err(error) => {
               manager.shutdown().await?;
               return Err(error);
         }
      }

      Ok(manager)
   }
   ```

   It calls `LogosSql::start(config).await?`, then checks whether the `credentials` table exists. If needed, it submits `CREATE TABLE` through Logos SQL. A later participant obtains the schema by replaying channel history.

1. Then, open `config.rs`. This file handles constructing `LogosSqlConfig`, with signing and funding credentials in `WriterConfig`:

   ```rust
   /// Parses startup options and builds the `λSQL` configuration.
   pub fn from_args() -> AppResult<(LogosSqlConfig, Encryption)> {
      let options = Options::parse();
      let encryption =
         Encryption::from_file(&options.encryption_key_file, options.channel_id.as_ref())?;

      let config = LogosSqlConfig {
         channel_id: options.channel_id,
         node_url: options.node_url,
         writer: Some(WriterConfig {
               publication: PublicationConfig::default(),
               signing_key: options.signing_key,
               funding: FundingConfig {
                  funding_pk: options.funding_key,
                  change_pk: None,
                  max_tx_fee: options.max_tx_fee.into(),
                  priority_fee_percent: options.priority_fee_percent,
               },
         }),
         state_dir: options.state_dir,
      };

      Ok((config, encryption))
   }
   ```   
   
   Publication settings control batching and queue limits. The library drives replication in the background; the application does not run a separate [Zone SDK](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#zone-sdk) event loop.

   > **Note**
   >
   > Encryption belongs to the application, not `LogosSqlConfig`. The example uses XChaCha20-Poly1305 from RustCrypto to encrypt each field and detect tampering. It stores the nonce with the encrypted value; the key stays in the local key file and is never submitted to Logos SQL.

## Step 3: Add and read a credential

1. At the prompt in terminal A, enter:

   ```text
   add email demo@example.org not-a-real-password
   ```

   **Expected result:** `committed locally as <tx-id>; not final`. The transaction ID varies. This confirms a local commit, not publication or finality.

1. Read the credential:

   ```text
   show email
   ```

   **Expected result:**

   ```text
   email
     account: demo@example.org
     password: not-a-real-password
     notes:
   ```

### Understand how it works

1. Find `prepare_credential_insert` in `passwords.rs`:

   ```rust
   fn prepare_credential_insert(credential: &StoredCredential) -> TransactionBuilder {
       TransactionBuilder::new(
           "INSERT INTO credentials (label, account, password, notes)
            VALUES (?1, ?2, ?3, ?4)",
       )
       .bind(&credential.label)
       .bind(credential.account.as_slice())
       .bind(credential.password.as_slice())
       .bind(credential.notes.as_slice())
   }
   ```

1. In the same file, find the application's `add` method. It encrypts the account, password and initially empty notes into a `StoredCredential`:
   
   ```rust
   /// Adds one credential.
   ///
   /// Concurrent attempts to use the same label produce a primary-key
   /// conflict.
   pub async fn add(&self, label: String, account: String, password: String) -> AppResult<TxId> {
      let credential = StoredCredential {
         account: self.encryption.encrypt(&label, "account", &account)?,
         password: self.encryption.encrypt(&label, "password", &password)?,
         notes: self.encryption.encrypt(&label, "notes", "")?,
         label,
      };

      Ok(self
         .logos_sql
         .execute(prepare_credential_insert(&credential))
         .await?)
   }
   ```

   Each `bind` above supplies the next parameter through the standard `rusqlite::ToSql` interface: a readable label and three encrypted binary values. The app then passes this builder to `self.logos_sql.execute(...).await?`.

   > **Tip**
   >
   > For multiple statements in one SQL transaction, append `.query(sql)` and its bindings. They commit or roll back together under one transaction ID. The library owns `BEGIN` and `COMMIT`; do not include them in the SQL.

1. Find `credential` in the same file:

   ```rust
   /// Reads one credential from the local `SQLite` database.
   pub fn credential(&self, label: &str) -> AppResult<Option<Credential>> {
      self.stored_credential(label)?
         .map(|credential| credential.decrypt(&self.encryption))
         .transpose()
   }

   fn stored_credential(&self, label: &str) -> AppResult<Option<StoredCredential>> {
      if !self.schema_exists()? {
         return Ok(None);
      }

      let connection = self.logos_sql.read_connection()?;

      let mut statement = connection.prepare(
         "SELECT label, account, password, notes
            FROM credentials WHERE label = ?1",
      )?;

      Ok(statement
         .query_row([label], |row| {
               Ok(StoredCredential {
                  label: row.get("label")?,
                  account: row.get("account")?,
                  password: row.get("password")?,
                  notes: row.get("notes")?,
               })
         })
         .optional()?)
   }
   ```

 It calls `stored_credential`, which opens `self.logos_sql.read_connection()?` and queries `credentials` with ordinary SQLite calls. The app decrypts the fields before displaying them. Reads use the local database, not a network request.

## Step 4: Read from another participant

1. In terminal B, enter the same source checkout and repeat only the `export` commands from [Step 2](#step-2-configure-and-start-the-application). They reuse the existing `channel-signing.pem` and `password-manager.key` files. Do not generate new keys: both instances must use the same channel and encryption key. On separate machines, each instance needs a securely transferred copy of the encryption key.

   The example has no read-only startup mode: both instances have writer credentials, even when you only issue read commands. Keep these test credentials on your own machine.

1. Start a second instance with a different directory:

   ```bash
   ./target/release/examples/password_manager --state-dir ./password-manager-b
   ```

1. At its prompt, enter `show email`.

   **Expected result:** the same account and fake password appear. If it prints `credential not found`, leave both processes running and try again after the write reaches this participant.

   Each instance has its own SQLite database. The schema and data arrive through channel history; no database files are copied between them. Seeing the row here confirms replication, not finality.

## Step 5: Update the password and notes

1. In terminal A, enter:

   ```text
   update email another-fake-password
   notes email recovery codes stored separately
   ```

   **Expected result:** each command reports `committed locally as <tx-id>; not final`.

1. In terminal B, run `show email` again until both changes appear. Run `list` to see the label and account:

   ```text
   email (demo@example.org)
   ```

### Understand how it works

1. Find `prepare_password_update` in `passwords.rs`:

   ```rust
   fn prepare_password_update(label: &str, password: &[u8], old_password: &[u8]) -> TransactionBuilder {
       TransactionBuilder::new(
           "UPDATE credentials SET password = ?2
            WHERE label = ?1 AND password = ?3",
       )
       .bind(label)
       .bind(password)
       .bind(old_password)
   }
   ```

   The application reads the stored password, checks it can decrypt it, and encrypts the replacement. The SQL compares the original encrypted bytes with the bytes still in the row; it does not decrypt them. Notes updates check the old notes independently, so changing the notes does not invalidate the password condition. Deletes check all the entry's stored values as read when the command was prepared.

   These conditions stay with the original SQL if the user retries a displaced write. The retry reuses the saved encrypted values, rather than encrypting them again. A condition that no longer matches changes no rows; SQLite still considers that successful. Check the resulting data rather than treating a transaction ID as proof that a value changed.

## Step 6: Review a displaced write

This step applies if channel history changes and the application reports displaced writes. The commands above do not deliberately create a fork, so an ordinary run may have none.

1. Enter `displacements` to list writes awaiting review. If there are none, it prints `no displacements awaiting review`.

   While any remain, ordinary new writes are blocked. A blocked write prints an error and directs the user to `displacements`, then `show` or `list` to inspect the data.

1. Inspect the current entry with `show email`. Decide whether the original operation should still be attempted.

1. Choose one action for an ID from the list, replacing `<tx-id>`:

   | Command | Effect |
   | --- | --- |
   | `retry <tx-id>` | Executes the saved SQL with its original conditions and marks that displacement handled after success. |
   | `handle <tx-id>` | Marks the displacement handled without submitting another write. |

   A retry prints `retry committed locally as <new-tx-id>; not final`. Use `show` to check the data afterwards. If the selected displacement has changed since it was listed, refresh `displacements` and review it again.

   This example leaves retries to the user. Other applications can handle displacements automatically when their SQL conditions and application policy make that safe. Handling a displacement does not cancel the original write; it can return after another reorganisation.

1. Check `displacements` again before continuing. If another displacement arrives during review, the next ordinary write remains blocked until that item is handled too.

   See [Handle displaced writes](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/logos-sql/handle-displaced-writes.md) for the underlying library calls and how to add this flow to another application.

## Step 7: Remove the entry and stop

1. In terminal A, enter `remove email`.

1. In terminal B, run `show email` until it prints `credential not found`.

   If the entry keeps appearing, run `displacements` in terminal A. If the removal is listed, review it as described in [Step 6](#step-6-review-a-displaced-write).

1. Enter `exit` in both terminals. The example calls `shutdown().await` to stop replication. Shutdown does not wait for finality.

1. Restart either instance with its original command and state directory, then enter `list`.

   **Expected result:** it resumes from saved state and follows the channel. If the deletion remains in the current history, `email` is absent. A chain reorganisation can still change non-finalised data.

## Troubleshooting

### Startup prints nothing and does not return

`LogosSql::start` processes channel history before it returns, so the example is silent while it catches up—a few minutes is normal on a local node, even when everything is configured correctly. If the prompt has not appeared after that, check that the node is running, that it reports `mode: Online`, and that `LOGOS_SQL_NODE_URL` matches its `api.backend.listen_address`. The state directory is created before the first connection attempt, so finding database files there does not mean startup succeeded.

### A credential cannot be decrypted

Check that both instances use the same encryption key file contents and channel. A wrong key or modified encrypted data causes decryption to fail. Do not generate a replacement key to fix this: a new key cannot decrypt existing entries.

Use a fresh channel and state directory for this encrypted example. It does not migrate old unencrypted entries or rotate keys. Encrypting future writes cannot hide unencrypted data already published in the channel history.

### Adding a credential reports a primary key constraint error

The label already exists. Use `show` to inspect it, `update` to change its password, or choose another label for a new entry.

### The second instance does not show a change

Check that both instances follow the same channel, that the node is processing blocks, and that the writer has valid signing authority and funding. Keep both processes running and issue the read command again. The terminal does not refresh displayed results automatically.

### A request returns PublishPending

The pending-write queue is full or the library is still saving an accepted publication. The new request has not committed any SQL changes. Leave replication running and try that request later; do not assume other errors have the same retry guarantee.

### A read needs finalised data

The example reads the latest local state. Applications needing settled history can use `finalized_read_connection()` with the same SQLite API. The schema and each data change appear in that view only after their writes finalise.

---

> Source: https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/logos-sql/handle-displaced-writes
> Markdown index of all Logos docs: https://docs.logos.co/llms.txt

# Handle displaced writes

#### Find out why a Logos SQL write was blocked, review displaced writes and decide how to continue.

> **Tip: Version**
>
> This document is accurate for **Testnet v0.3**.

A write can succeed in your local database but later be removed: another writer may publish before it, or a blockchain reorganisation may replace the branch containing it. Logos SQL reports that write as displaced and blocks new writes until the application has reviewed it.

Review does not have to involve a user. An application can automatically retry writes designed to remain safe after other changes, or mark them handled if they are no longer needed. The [password-manager example](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/logos-sql/build-application-with-logos-sql.md) leaves retry decisions to the user.

The flow is: catch the blocked-write error, list the displaced writes, inspect the current data, then retry or continue without each write. The [password-manager guide](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/logos-sql/build-application-with-logos-sql.md) shows the terminal commands for this. This page explains the library calls behind them.

> **Info: Prerequisites**
>
>
> - A running `LogosSql` writer and access to its current database.
> - An application write path that calls `execute` and handles its result.
>

## What to expect

- You can identify local writes that need an application decision.
- You can retry a selected write or mark it handled without retrying it.
- You can keep the review correct when more displacements arrive in the meantime.

## Step 1: Recognise a blocked write

1. When submitting a transaction, handle `Error::UnhandledDisplacements` separately from other errors:

   ```rust
   use logos_sql::Error;

   match db.execute(transaction).await {
       Ok(tx_id) => println!("Committed locally as {tx_id}"),
       Err(Error::UnhandledDisplacements) => {
           println!("Earlier writes were displaced. Review them before continuing.");
       }
       Err(error) => return Err(error.into()),
   }
   ```

   This error means earlier writes need review. The new transaction has not run, and no changes from it were committed.

1. Pause ordinary submissions and show the review flow below. Reads still work, so the application can inspect what is in the database now.

## Step 2: Find out what was displaced

1. Fetch the writes awaiting review:

   ```rust
   let displacements = db.unhandled_displacements().await?;

   for displacement in &displacements {
       println!("{}: {:?}", displacement.tx_id, displacement.reason);
   }
   ```

   Each entry identifies one of this participant's writes by its transaction ID and gives the reason it was displaced.

   With multiple writers, another participant's writes can arrive while yours are still waiting to be published. A chain reorganisation can also remove accepted writes, even with only one writer. The reasons below distinguish writes removed from [channel](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#channel) history from those removed while still waiting locally:

   | Reason | Meaning |
   | --- | --- |
   | `Orphaned` | The [Zone SDK](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#zone-sdk) removed a previously tracked write from channel history, for example because a competing channel write replaced it. This can happen without a blockchain reorganisation. |
   | `PendingWriteInvalidated` | The write was still waiting locally to be published when other channel writes or a chain reorganisation changed the database it was based on. Logos SQL removed the local write rather than automatically applying it again to the changed data. |

   Neither reason means the SQL failed a constraint. Even writes to unrelated rows can compete for a channel position.

1. Use the transaction ID to identify the original operation, then read the current data. In the password manager example, the user can use `show` or `list` before deciding what to do.

   > **Tip**
   >
   > If your application needs descriptions such as “changed the email password”, save that description with the transaction ID when preparing the original write. The builder exposes it through `transaction.tx_id()`. Save the association persistently if it must survive restart. Logos SQL already retains the SQL needed for a retry; the application does not need to store another copy.

1. Keep the returned `Displacement` value for the retry or handle call. It identifies the specific item you reviewed, so an old action cannot clear a newer displacement of the same write.

   A write that returns to live history or finalises no longer appears in the review list. Refresh the list before showing old review items after a long pause or restart.

## Step 3: Retry or continue without the write

Choose separately for each displaced write. The password manager asks the user; another application may have a policy for particular operations.

1. Compare the intended operation with the current data. Choose whether to retry its original SQL, leave it without a retry, or prepare a different change.

   For example, the password manager checks that the stored password still matches the encrypted value the application originally read:

   ```rust
   fn prepare_password_update(
       label: &str,
       password: &[u8],
       old_password: &[u8],
   ) -> TransactionBuilder {
       TransactionBuilder::new(
           "UPDATE credentials SET password = ?2
            WHERE label = ?1 AND password = ?3",
       )
       .bind(label)
       .bind(password)
       .bind(old_password)
   }
   ```

   - Both parameters contain encrypted bytes. The application encrypts the replacement before preparing the SQL and keeps the original stored bytes for the condition. A retry reuses both values without encrypting them again.
   - The condition and update execute together. Changes to notes or other entries do not affect this condition. If this entry's stored password is different, the statement changes no rows.
   - SQLite considers zero matching rows successful. `execute` returns a transaction ID, not an affected-row count, so success alone does not tell the application whether this update changed the password.

1. Decide which operations the application can retry automatically. Their SQL conditions should express the assumptions that must still hold, and the application must decide what to do when those conditions fail.

   The password-manager example uses manual review as its policy. Logos SQL does not require a person to make this decision; applications can use the same retry and handle calls automatically where appropriate.

Once you have decided, use one of the following calls for the selected `displacement`.

### Option A—Retry the original SQL

1. Pass the selected entry to the retry method:

   ```rust
   use logos_sql::Error;

   match db.retry_displacement(&displacement).await {
       Ok(new_tx_id) => println!("Retry committed locally as {new_tx_id}"),
       Err(Error::StaleDisplacement) => {
           // A reorganisation may have made the branch containing this write
           // canonical again. Fetch the updated list before retrying.
       }
       Err(error) => return Err(error.into()),
   }
   ```

   A successful call executes the original SQL and parameters, creates a new transaction ID and marks the selected displacement handled. This is allowed while other displacements await review. Time and random functions are evaluated again for the new write.

   If the call fails or is interrupted, the retry may already have committed. Do not respond to every error by submitting the same operation again.

### Option B—Continue without retrying the original SQL

1. Mark the selected entry handled:

   ```rust
   db.mark_displacement_handled(displacement).await?;
   ```

   This records that the application has considered it. No replacement write is submitted. Once the remaining displacements are handled, the application may submit a different transaction based on the current data.

> **Warning: Marking handled does not withdraw the write**
>
> Marking a displacement handled clears the application's review item; it does not erase the write from the branch that contained it. If that branch becomes canonical again, Logos SQL rebuilds the database from its history and the write returns, even if the application chose not to retry it.

## Step 4: Continue writing

1. Refresh `unhandled_displacements()` after handling the reviewed items. A newly arrived displacement still needs a decision even if you finished an earlier batch.

1. Re-read the data needed for subsequent writes and prepare them again where necessary. Coordinate this with other application tasks that submit writes.

   The write block belongs to the whole participant. Once the list is clear, it does not protect another task from submitting work prepared before the displacement.

1. Submit the next operation and continue to handle `Error::UnhandledDisplacements`. A new displacement can arrive between the list query and the write; the execution check will block that write if it does.

## Troubleshooting

### A reviewed item returns StaleDisplacement

The selected occurrence was handled, cleared or replaced before the retry. Refresh the list. Do not retry it through ordinary `execute` to bypass this check.

### Writes remain blocked after review

Check the current review list. Another displacement may have arrived while the application was reviewing earlier entries. Handling an earlier entry does not clear the new one.

### A handled write becomes live again

This can happen when the chain returns to a branch containing the original write. Use `write_status(tx_id)` and current database reads to update the application's view. Handling a displacement records a local decision, not a permanent chain outcome.

---

> Source: https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/faq
> Markdown index of all Logos docs: https://docs.logos.co/llms.txt

# Blockchain FAQ

#### Review answers to less obvious questions about how the Logos Blockchain works and where it fits.

> **Info**
>
> This document reflects the state of this Logos component as it will exist on mainnet. Some features described here may not be available on the current testnet.

## How is the Logos Blockchain private if Mantle notes are public UTXOs?

It is important to distinguish between two distinct kinds of privacy that are possible on the [Logos Blockchain](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#logos-blockchain): transaction privacy, and proposer privacy. Transaction privacy obscures transactions and other information published on-chain, preventing third parties from learning what exactly an individual did when interacting with the blockchain. On the other hand, proposer privacy makes it difficult to link a proposed block to whoever proposed it: it is computationally infeasible for an observer to determine which participant is behind a given block, either before or after it's added to the chain. In other words, **transaction privacy hides the data published to the chain, while proposer privacy protects the people running the infrastructure**. The latter is particularly relevant for Proof of Stake blockchains, which select block proposers according to a schedule generated ahead of time.

Because the Logos Blockchain's Bedrock layer (which maintains the [Mantle ledger](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/concepts/about-mantle.md#mantle-ledger)) serves a resilient foundational layer for apps running on Logos Zones, it is designed primarily to protect the privacy of block proposers. If proposers could be identified or connected with transactions included in their blocks, they could become targets for coercion or denial of service attacks by hostile actors. Even when there is no credible threat of being targeted, block proposers without privacy could engage in cautionary self-censorship by excluding certain transactions, thereby compromising the neutrality of the entire network. Protecting proposer privacy helps prevent this regardless of how transparent the ledger is.

Transaction privacy needs differ vastly for different use cases, so this type of privacy is not provided directly by Bedrock for most cases. [Notes](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#note) and their transfers are recorded openly on the ledger, similar to Bitcoin, and the Bedrock layer makes no attempt to hide that data. Despite this, it is possible to mine new notes and write arbitrary data on-chain in a private way by submitting these types of transactions via the [Blend Network](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#blend-network). Bedrock therefore supports privacy-preserving consensus participation and [inscriptions](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#inscription), but not note transfers or other transaction types.

Developers that need to protect their app's data, such as balances or message contents, must implement their desired level of transaction privacy at the [Zone](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/concepts/about-zones.md) layer instead of relying on Bedrock for it. **Transaction privacy is supported natively on the [LEZ](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#lez), in addition to public transactions**.

> **Note**
>
> For more information on proposer privacy on Logos, see [Anonymous Block Proposers](https://blog.logos.co/article/anonymous-block-proposers).

## Does the Blend Network always protect proposer privacy for everyone?

No, that protection depends on whether the proposer is a [core node](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#core-node), and how many other core nodes are active in a given [epoch](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#epoch). Only declared core nodes relay and blend messages, and their participation in Blend activity makes it hard to distinguish when they publish their own proposals. A block proposer that hasn't declared as a core node participates as an edge node instead, sending its proposal through core nodes for blending - an unusual activity that can be singled out and connected to published blocks by some attackers. If too few core nodes are active, all proposers fall back to broadcasting directly, with no Blend privacy for that epoch.

## If Bedrock doesn't interpret Zone data, what secures funds bridged into a Zone?

Correctness is the Zone's own responsibility, not Bedrock's. [Bedrock](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/concepts/about-bedrock.md) stores whatever state updates a [Zone](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/concepts/about-zones.md)'s sequencer inscribes without verifying their validity, so each Zone chooses its own correctness mechanism - publishing zero knowledge validity proofs, running a fraud-proof challenge window, or requiring its nodes to re-execute the state transition themselves. For bridged funds specifically, Bedrock enforces only one aggregate invariant: the total note value withdrawn from a Zone can never exceed the total value deposited into it. It doesn't verify that a withdrawal went to the correct account or that a Zone's internal accounting is honest - that guarantee comes entirely from whichever correctness mechanism the Zone itself implements.

On the LEZ, transactions are verified differently depending on if they're public or private. Public transactions are re-executed by LEZ validators, while private transactions involve the generation of zero knowledge proofs via Risc0, which are then verified by LEZ validators.

## Does decentralised sequencing eliminate MEV on a Zone?

No, it distributes the opportunity for MEV extraction across a set of sequencers rather than removing it. When a Zone uses several sequencers, taking turns on a round-robin schedule or competing to publish first, no single sequencer can reliably capture all of the MEV available the way a single-sequencer rollup's operator could. A threshold of sequencers can also jointly sign a change to the sequencer list, letting an honest majority remove a malicious one.

By isolating MEV to the Zone level, the Logos Blockchain is able to remain neutral and decentralised - centralised sequencing in one Zone does not impact the decentalisation of other Zones.

## Why build on a Zone instead of launching an independent Layer 1?

Launching a new Layer 1 means bootstrapping its own validator set, economic security, and data availability from scratch, which a young chain typically struggles to do. Building as a [Zone](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/concepts/about-zones.md) instead lets an application keep full control over its own state and execution environment while relying on the Logos Blockchain for consensus guarantees and data availability it couldn't easily provide on its own. A Zone isn't locked into using Bedrock's other features to get this: it can run as a fully independent sovereign rollup, using Bedrock only for ordering and data availability, or opt into decentralised sequencing and token bridging for extra interoperability without giving up the sovereign rollup model's benefits.

---

> Source: https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/reference/blockchain-api-reference
> Markdown index of all Logos docs: https://docs.logos.co/llms.txt

# Logos Blockchain API Reference

This page describes every HTTP endpoint a [Logos Blockchain](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#logos-blockchain) node exposes. It's accurate for Logos Blockchain node `0.3.1`.

> **Tip**
>
> If you have access to a running Blockchain node, you can view the OpenAPI specification at `/api-docs/openapi.json` and a Swagger UI at `/swagger-ui/` on the same port.

## Conventions

- The API listens on `127.0.0.1:8080` by default. To change the address, set `api.backend.listen_address` in the node's configuration.
- Requests and responses use JSON unless an endpoint says otherwise. Send request bodies with the `Content-Type: application/json` header.
- A few successful responses have a JSON body but a `text/plain` content type: [`GET /leader/aged-notes`](#get-leaderaged-notes), [`GET /leader/claim/vouchers`](#get-leaderclaimvouchers), [`GET /wallet/{public_key}/balance`](#get-walletpublic_keybalance), and [`POST /wallet/transactions/transfer-funds`](#post-wallettransactionstransfer-funds). Parse the body as JSON regardless of the content type.
- Hashes, block IDs, transaction IDs, [note](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#note) IDs, declaration IDs, and ZK public keys are 32-byte values encoded as 64-character hexadecimal strings without a `0x` prefix.
- Peer IDs are libp2p peer IDs encoded as base58 strings. Network addresses and [locators](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#locator) are libp2p `multiaddr` strings, such as `/ip4/203.0.113.10/udp/3000/quic-v1`.
- [Slots](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#slot), [epochs](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#epoch), and token amounts are unsigned integers.
- Path parameters are shown in braces. For example, in `GET /cryptarchia/blocks/{id}`, replace `{id}` with a block ID.

### Access and security

The API has no authentication. Anyone who can reach it can read the node's wallet balances, sign arbitrary transaction hashes with the node's keys, and spend its funds. Keep the API bound to `127.0.0.1`, or put it behind an authenticating proxy, and don't expose it to the public internet.

### Error responses

When the node handles a request and it fails, the response has a non-`200` status code and the following body:

| Field | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `code` | integer | The HTTP status code of the response. |
| `message` | string | A human-readable description of the error. |

Most failures return `500`. Endpoints that look up a single item return `404` when the item doesn't exist, and [`GET /cryptarchia/blocks_range`](#get-cryptarchiablocks_range) returns `400` for invalid query parameters.

Some errors don't use this body:

- A malformed path parameter, query string, or request body returns `400`, `415`, or `422` with a plain-text message, such as `Failed to deserialize query string: missing field 'slot_from'`.
- An unknown path returns `404` with an empty body.
- A request that takes longer than the API timeout returns `408` with an empty body. The timeout is 30 seconds by default. To change it, set `api.backend.timeout`, in seconds, in the node's configuration.

### Requests while the node is bootstrapping

While the node is in the `Bootstrapping` state, the following endpoints don't respond until the node is `Online`. Each request waits until the API timeout and then returns `408`:

- [`GET /blend/info`](#get-blendinfo)
- [`GET /blend/transactions/pending`](#get-blendtransactionspending)
- [`GET /pow/status`](#get-powstatus)
- [`GET /pow/rewards/claimable`](#get-powrewardsclaimable)
- [`POST /pow/claim`](#post-powclaim)

The other read endpoints on this page respond normally while the node is [bootstrapping](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#bootstrapping).

## Node

### `GET /version`

Gets the version and build information of the running node.

#### Response fields

| Field | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `version` | string | The version of the node binary, such as `0.3.1`. |
| `commit` | string or `null` | The abbreviated commit the binary was built from. `null` if it wasn't built from a Git checkout. |
| `tag` | string or `null` | The Git tag that points at that commit. `null` if there is none. |
| `target` | string | The target triple the binary was compiled for, such as `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`. |
| `profile` | string | The Cargo profile the binary was compiled with, such as `release`. |
| `rustc` | string | The version of the Rust compiler that built the binary. |

### `GET /chain/id`

Gets the ID of the chain the node runs on. The chain ID is fixed by the node's deployment and doesn't change while the node runs.

#### Response fields

| Field | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `chain_id` | string | The chain ID. |

## Consensus

### `GET /cryptarchia/info`

Gets the consensus state information for the node.

#### Response fields

| Field | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cryptarchia_info` | object | The node's current view of the chain. |
| `cryptarchia_info.lib` | string | The ID of the latest immutable block (LIB), the most recent block that can no longer be reorganised. |
| `cryptarchia_info.lib_slot` | integer | The slot of the latest immutable block. |
| `cryptarchia_info.tip` | string | The ID of the block at the tip of the node's canonical chain. |
| `cryptarchia_info.slot` | integer | The slot of the tip block. |
| `cryptarchia_info.height` | integer | The height of the tip block, which is the length of the canonical chain. |
| `cryptarchia_info.state` | string | The state of the consensus engine: `Bootstrapping` or `Online`. |
| `phase` | string | The phase the chain service is in. See the following table. |

`phase` has one of the following values:

| Value | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `AwaitingGenesisTime` | The genesis time is in the future. The node serves only read-only queries. |
| `InitialBlockDownload` | The node applies blocks while it waits for the Initial Block Download to complete. |
| `ProlongedBootstrapPeriod` | The Prolonged Bootstrap Period is running. |
| `Following` | The node follows the chain in real time. |

### `GET /time/info`

Gets the node's slot and epoch timing information.

#### Response fields

| Field | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `slot_duration_ms` | integer | The duration of a slot, in milliseconds. |
| `genesis_time_unix_ms` | integer | The genesis time of the chain, in milliseconds since the Unix epoch. |
| `current_slot` | integer | The current slot. |
| `current_epoch` | integer | The current epoch. |
| `slots_per_epoch` | integer | The number of slots in an epoch. |

### `GET /cryptarchia/headers`

Gets the IDs of the blocks on a branch of the chain, walking from a descendant block back towards an ancestor.

#### Query parameters

| Parameter | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `from` | string | No | The ID of the block to start from. Defaults to the tip of the node's canonical chain. |
| `to` | string | No | The ID of the ancestor block to stop at. Defaults to the latest immutable block. |

#### Response

An array of block IDs, newest first, including both `from` and `to`. The response contains at most 512 IDs.

### `GET /cryptarchia/blocks/{id}`

Gets a block by its ID.

#### Path parameters

| Parameter | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | string | The ID of the block. |

#### Response fields

Returns `404` if the node doesn't store the block.

| Field | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `header` | object | The block header. |
| `header.id` | string | The ID of the block. |
| `header.parent_block` | string | The ID of the parent block. |
| `header.slot` | integer | The slot the block was proposed in. |
| `header.body_root` | string | The root of the block body's Merkle tree. |
